question_text:
In maritime law, the principle of 'salvage' rewards individuals who recover sunken vessels or cargo, with the reward proportional to the value of the property saved. Historically, this system has incentivized the recovery of many historically significant shipwrecks. However, a recent ruling by the International Tribunal for the Law of the Sea has expanded the definition of 'abandoned' shipwrecks to include those whose original owners can no longer be reasonably identified, even if the wreck was previously considered property of a state or private entity. Consequently, professional salvors argue that this ruling will substantially reduce the number of salvage operations undertaken, because it increases the legal uncertainty over whether a salvor can retain a claim to the recovered property. Therefore, it is likely that fewer historically significant shipwrecks will be recovered in the coming decades.

Which of the following, if true, most seriously weakens the argument above?
